title: Same Eye, Different Wiring
paragraphs: Octopuses and humans last shared an ancestor hundreds of millions of years ago, a creature that almost certainly lacked a camera eye. Yet both lineages ended up with camera eyes: a lens focusing light onto a retina at the back of a chamber. Biologists call this convergent evolution, the independent arrival of unrelated organisms at similar solutions.

The resemblance is impressive, but the differences are more revealing. In the vertebrate eye, the nerve fibres run across the front of the retina and must pass back through it to reach the brain, which leaves a small blind spot where no light can be detected. The octopus retina is wired the other way round, with its receptors facing the incoming light, and it has no such gap. Two designs that look alike from outside turn out to carry the marks of entirely separate histories.

Convergence is not confined to eyes. Bats and toothed whales both locate prey by echolocation, and wings have evolved separately in birds, bats and the extinct pterosaurs. Such cases have fed a long argument about predictability. Stephen Jay Gould suggested that if the tape of life were replayed, the outcome would likely differ, because history is shaped by countless contingent events. The palaeontologist Simon Conway Morris has instead argued that convergence is pervasive in evolution.

The two positions are less opposed than they first appear. Convergence can make broad outcomes such as eyes, wings or sonar likely without making any particular eye predictable, and the octopus and the human illustrate both halves of that claim at once. Both arrived at the camera eye, yet the wiring of each was settled by its own particular ancestry.

Read this way, convergence is less a verdict on whether evolution repeats itself than a reminder to ask at what level of detail the question is being posed. Answer it at one level and life looks inevitable; answer it at another and it looks like an accident.

sources.claim: Kafadanbacaklılar (ahtapot) ve omurgalılarda kamera tipi göz bağımsız olarak evrimleşmiştir; yarasalar ve dişli balinalarda ekolokasyon, kuşlar, yarasalar ve pterozorlarda kanat yakınsak evrim örnekleridir.

Omurgalı retinasında sinir lifleri fotoreseptörlerin önünden geçer ve optik sinirin retinadan çıktığı yerde kör nokta oluşur; kafadanbacaklıların retinası ters düzende olduğundan böyle bir kör noktaları yoktur.
Stephen Jay Gould 'yaşamın bandını yeniden oynatma' düşünce deneyiyle evrimde olumsallığı vurguladı.
Paleontolog Simon Conway Morris yakınsamanın evrimde yaygın olduğunu savunur.
